segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: What's up Beth? You look a little sad.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Well, recently I've been spending lots of time with my cat and houseplants,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: if you know what I mean. I'm feeling a bit lonely.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: It might help to know that you're not the only one feeling lonely.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Loneliness has been called the modern epidemic.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Although millions of us live together in towns and cities,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: more and more people report feeling lonely and unconnected to those they live close to.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Loneliness can affect anyone.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And while everyone's experience of loneliness is different, its effects can be serious.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Research has shown that loneliness puts people at greater risk of many health issues,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: including dementia and heart disease.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, how can loneliness be fixed?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In this programme, we'll be hearing about one project in the Netherlands aiming to do just that.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And, as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary as well.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here in the UK, an organisation called The Campaign to End Loneliness

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: has been offering advice and support since 2011.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, according to the campaign,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: what proportion of British adults

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: report feeling lonely at least some of the time?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Is it a 29 b 39 or c 49

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Erm I would guess it 39

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK Beth I reveal the answer later in the programme

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Feeling lonely is not necessarily the same as being alone.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Some people can happily spend lots of time on their own,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: while others may be surrounded by people but still feel disconnected.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So, what do we mean when we say we feel lonely?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Myra Anubi, presenter of BBC World Service programme

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: People Fixing the World, explaining what loneliness means to her.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: It's that feeling when you crave people's company

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and you find it hard to connect,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: or maybe you just feel left out with no one to turn to.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Now, feeling lonely isn't just uncomfortable.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: When it's experienced over time, it's been associated with health issues

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: like a higher risk of having depression, dementia or even heart disease.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: When we're lonely, we crave people's company. We want their company a lot.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: We might also feel left out unhappy because we're not included in what others are doing.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And maybe we have no one to turn to no one we can go to and ask for support and help.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Someone who suffered all these feelings was Bep de Bruyn.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In 2013, Bep, aged 74, was found dead at her home in Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Her death wasn't suspicious, but it shocked the whole country because it turned out she'd been dead for 10 years.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Bep had lost contact with her only child and kept to herself in her apartment So when she died sometime in 2003 no one realised

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Bepp tragic story inspired a national campaign to combat loneliness

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: including one project called Oma's Soup,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: a kitchen bringing lonely elderly people together with schoolchildren and students to make soup.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Oma means grandma in Dutch and the project encourages young people to spend time with their grandparents' generation.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here, Claire Bates, reporter for BBC World Service programme People Fixing the World, explains how the project got started.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, it's run by two young guys called Max Cranendijk and Martin Canters.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And now they were concerned their grandparents' generation were becoming isolated and lonely.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And meanwhile, they had lots of student friends who had free time,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: so they thought, why not try to bring these two generations together through making soup?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Omar's Soup was started by Max and Martin, two local guys, or men.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: They wanted to involve their student friends because they had lots of free time,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: time when they do not have to work or study and can do what they want.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Max and Martin found the perfect way to help elderly people who felt lonely

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: by bringing them together with students.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you bring someone together, you help people or groups to become friendly or to do something together, especially something they wouldn't usually do, like make soup.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Omar soup has been a big success and has spread to other cities across the Netherlands including Rotterdam the hometown of Beb de Brun making her tragic death the spark for something much more hopeful

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I think it's time to reveal the answer to your question, Neil.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Right. I asked you what proportion of British adults report feeling lonely at least some of the time.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I said it was 39%.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Which was the wrong answer, I'm afraid, Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: sadly, the correct answer is even higher 49% of adults, that's around 26 million people in the UK,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: making it even more important to reach out and connect with others.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, it's time to recap the vocabulary we've learned in this programme,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: starting with the verb crave to have a strong wish or desire for something.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you feel left out, you're unhappy because you've been excluded from something.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: To turn to someone means to go to someone and ask them for help or support.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A guy is an informal way of saying a man.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Free time, also called leisure time, is time when you do not have to work or study and can do what you want.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And finally, the phrasal verb, to bring someone together, means to help people or groups become friendly or do something together, especially if they usually don't.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But if you're feeling lonely, remember you're not alone.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So reach out by joining us again next time here at 6 Minute English.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Bye.
